edges.mechanism: Complementary anti-androgen action in scalp: finasteride inhibits 5α-reductase (DHT formation), while topical 17α-estradiol shifts follicular androgen metabolism toward weaker estrogens/aromatase (its effect is reportedly NOT via 5α-reductase). Commonly co-formulated for androgenetic alopecia.
edges.evidence: Retrospective/comparative human AGA studies combining the two (both with minoxidil); topical finasteride outperformed topical 17α-estradiol. Skin-cell metabolism study showing 17α-estradiol does not act via 5α-reductase.

edges.mechanism: Dual 5α-reductase inhibition complements 17α-estradiol's follicular androgen-to-estrogen shift; used adjunctively in androgenetic alopecia.
edges.evidence: Human skin-cell androgen-metabolism study (dutasteride plus 17α-estradiol) and AGA treatment reviews; no dedicated combination efficacy trial.

edges.mechanism: Additive/complementary topical therapy for female pattern hair loss; different mechanisms (vasodilator/anagen inducer vs weak estrogen).
edges.evidence: Retrospective combination study and a randomized trial of estradiol+minoxidil vs minoxidil; head-to-head RCT found minoxidil the stronger agent and combination's added benefit non-significant, with more menstrual irregularity.

edges.mechanism: Overlapping estrogenic activity; 17α-estradiol is itself a component of conjugated equine estrogens and high systemic exposure can isomerize to the potent 17β-estradiol, giving additive estrogenic effect/feminization risk.
edges.evidence: Conjugated-equine-estrogen pharmacology reviews; primate study showing dose-dependent feminization via isomerization to 17β-estradiol.

edges.mechanism: Pharmacodynamic antagonism of estrogen-receptor-mediated effects; ER antagonism opposes hair-cycle and some metabolic actions (though part of 17α-estradiol neuroprotection is non-genomic and tamoxifen-insensitive).
edges.evidence: Mouse hair-cycle study (ER antagonist induces anagen), failed topical fulvestrant AGA trials, and cell neuroprotection only partly blocked by tamoxifen.

edges.mechanism: Both are weak/phyto-estrogens; co-exposure can be additive on estrogen-sensitive tissue, and phytoestrogens alter the CYP/COMT enzymes that metabolize 17α-estradiol.
edges.evidence: Rat study of 17α-estradiol plus genistein inhibiting prostate growth; MCF-7 study showing phytoestrogens modulate 17α-estradiol-metabolizing enzymes.

edges.mechanism: Mechanistic convergence as geroprotectors: both reduce mTORC1 activity, lower MEK-ERK (eIF4E) signalling and increase cap-independent translation. Overlap is mechanistic, not a tested combination (17α-estradiol effect is male-specific).
edges.evidence: Mouse mechanistic studies of shared cap-independent translation and MAPK regulation across rapamycin, acarbose and 17α-estradiol.

edges.mechanism: Co-members of the NIA Interventions Testing Program male-biased lifespan trio; overlapping male-specific glucose-handling, mTORC2 and MAPK mechanisms. Combined lifespan effect not tested.
edges.evidence: ITP lifespan studies and mechanistic work on male-specific glucose tolerance/mTORC2 signalling.

edges.mechanism: DHEA is a sex-steroid precursor that can be converted toward estrogens/androgens; theoretical additive hormonal effect with an estrogenic agent. No direct interaction study.
edges.evidence: Mechanistic/review inference from estrogen-signalling biology; no co-administration data.

edges.mechanism: Even a weak estrogen may stimulate estrogen-responsive tissue; 17α-estradiol was carcinogenic in neonatal mice and shows estrogenic activity in some assays (though it inhibits androgen-driven prostate tumor cells).
edges.evidence: Neonatal mouse carcinogenicity, uterotrophic/estrogen-responsive cell data, and review of estrogen biology; net precautionary.

edges.mechanism: Estrogenic agent with no human safety data; developmental estrogenic toxicity shown in animals. Approved topical label advises against use in pregnancy/breastfeeding.
edges.evidence: Ell-Cranell (alfatradiol) product information and neonatal mouse estrogen/carcinogen data.

edges.mechanism: Estrogens as a class are prothrombotic; any meaningful systemic estrogenic exposure could add thrombotic risk. Direct 17α-estradiol human VTE data are lacking.
edges.evidence: Mouse model of chronic estradiol+progesterone increasing experimental arterial/venous thrombosis; class-effect extrapolation.

edges.mechanism: 17α-estradiol is a near-identical structural epimer of 17β-estradiol; direct (unextracted) clinical estradiol immunoassays are prone to cross-reactivity/positive bias and could over-read estradiol, especially at low concentrations. Magnitude on named clinical analyzers is unquantified.
edges.evidence: Steroid immunoassay cross-reactivity analysis (low for most estrogen analogues on one platform) plus studies of direct E2 immunoassay bias/nonspecificity vs LC-MS/MS reference method.
